parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre or *inclāviāre, from Latin clāvis (“key”) or clāvus (“nail”) (see also clāvāre (“to nail”)). Probably influenced by cheie. Compare also Friulian inclavâ, French enclouer.
From încheia + -tură. Another proposed etymology was în + Vulgar Latin *clautūra, but this is less likely.

parole.significato: hither, here, this way, in my direction
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin in-(ec)cu(m) *hocce, from Latin hoc. Compare Megleno-Romanian ạncoatsi, coa, Dalmatian cauc.
From a Vulgar Latin root *incuneāre, from Latin cuneāre, ultimately from cuneus (“wedge”). Compare Albanian ngujoj. First attested in 1581.

parole.significato: to drive, goad (a horse); to chase away
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *incurrāre, from Latin incurrō, incurrere, from currō.
Either from Vulgar Latin incolicāre, from colus, or from a root *curricāre, from currō. Less likely from descurca, which is more likely derived from this word instead. First attested in 1581.
Probably from Vulgar Latin incallare, from Latin callēre (“be calloused, hardened, grow hard”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incaballicāre, from Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus (“nag, jade”). Compare Aromanian ncalic, ncãlicari or Albanian ngalkoj.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incalidīre. Compare Aromanian ncãldzãscu. Possibly also influenced by Latin incalēscō (whence încări).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *incarricāre, ultimately from Latin carrus. Compare Aromanian ãncarcu, ãncãrare, cf. also Albanian ngarkoj.
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *indemināre, from inde + minārī.

parole.significato: to stuff, cram, jam, pack, press in
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indensāre, from Latin densāre.
From fierbinte. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *inferventāre, from Latin fervens.

Unknown. Possibly from în + a Vulgar Latin root *fervidiāre, from Latin fervidus. Only appears in the 17th century writings of the scholar Dosoftei, who was known to have created some words, so the etymology is still uncertain.

From a Vulgar Latin *infebrizō or later Balkan Romance equivalent, derived from Latin febris. Cognate to Aromanian nhiuredz, nhiurari. The -ez type conjugation is likely the older variant due to the pronunciation of "io" in the root, as this pronunciation is an outcome of the intonation falling else
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *īnfīctus, from Latin īnfīxus. Doublet of infix.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *infrangere, from Latin infringere, from in- + frangō. Equivalent to în- + frânge. Compare Italian infrangere.

From a Vulgar Latin *infasciāre or în + Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia. Compare Aromanian nfash, nfãshari, Italian fasciare, Occitan faissar, French fesser, Portuguese enfaixar, Spanish fajar, Friulian infassâ, Venetan infasar, Istriot infasà, Sardinian fasciai.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingenuclāre < *ingenuculāre, from Latin geniculum. Compare Aromanian ndzinuclju, ndzinucljedzu, ndzinucljari, Italian inginocchiare, French agenouiller, Portuguese ajoelhar, Spanish ahinojar, Catalan agenollar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inglaciāre. Synchronically în- + gheață + -a.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingrevicāre, a verb based on early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem. Compare Aromanian ngricari.

parole.significato: to make or become heavy, burden
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *ingrevināre, from grevis, from Latin gravis. Compare Aromanian ngriunedz, ngriunari.

From gras or a Vulgar Latin root *ingrassiāre, from grassus, from Latin crassus (“thick, fat”). Compare Aromanian ngrash, ngrãshari, French engraisser, Dalmatian engrassur, Italian ingrassare, Spanish engrasar.

parole.significato: to imitate, mimic (a voice, etc), to echo
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (“trick, deceive, mock”) (attested in a gloss), from Latin *ganno or ganniō. Compare Aromanian angan, angãnari (“call”), Italian ingannare (“deceive, cheat”), Spanish engañar, Portuguese enganar, Catalan enganyar, Albanian gënjej. Cf. also Medieval
From în- + nota, the latter from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Aromanian (a)nutari, Italian nuotare.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ipsus or Latin ipsum, masculine accusative of ipse, with a nasal infix from Latin (compare attested inpsuius). Cognate with Aromanian nãs, Old French esse, Italian esso, Portuguese esse, Spanish ese, see more cognates at ipse.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin insignāre (also later attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin signō.

parole.significato: to marry, wed (become married or wedded)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(in)uxōrāre, a verb based on Latin uxor (“wife”). Compare Aromanian ãnsor, ãnsurari.

parole.significato: to repair the sole of a shoe
parole.testo: From în- + Vulgar Latin *solāre, from Latin solum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intītiō, from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intorcĕre, from Latin torquēre (cf. also intorquēre).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intreguāre, itself from Classical Latin interrogō. Doublet of the borrowing interoga.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intunicāre, from Latin tunicāre (“cover with a tunic”), from tunica (“tunic”). Compare Aromanian ãntunic, ãntunicari. Compare also Italian intonicare, Spanish entunicar (which were internal formations). Not related to întuneric.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *intenebricāre (attested in Medieval Latin), from Latin tenebricus. The original form may have been *întenerica before being influenced phonetically by or confused with the probably unrelated but coincidentally similar întuneca.

parole.significato: to stiffen, harden, make obstinate, rigid, inflexible
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *inversionāre, from Latin versiō, versiōnem (“turning, change”). Probably related to vierșun. Another proposed etymology is Hungarian verseny.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus. Doublet of involut.

From a Vulgar Latin *invitiāre, a variant of *vitiāre (“accustom, habituate, familiarize”), or formed from in- + Latin vitium (“vice”). Compare Aromanian anvets, nvets, anvitsari, Istro-Romanian ănmeţå, Italian avvezzare, invezzare, Spanish avezar, vezar, Portuguese vezar, Occitan envezar, Old Frenc
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Aromanian analtsu, anãltsari, Italian innalzare, Occitan enauçar, Old French enhaucier (where English enhance).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin serpis, from Latin serpēns, from serpō (“crawl, creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *serp-. Compare Aromanian sharpi.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excloppus (compare Aromanian shcljop, Albanian shqep, Occitan / Catalan esclop), from cloppus (compare Old French clop, also Italian zoppo).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *excloppitāre, from Late Latin excloppus, from cloppus. Cf. also Aromanian shcljoapic, shcljupicari.
From a Vulgar Latin root *zinzalus, from Late Latin zinzala or tentiala, of imitative origin. Compare Italian zanzara.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *titina.
From țară + -ână or Vulgar Latin terrīna, ultimately from terra (cf. the adjective terrēnus (“of the earth”); compare French terrine). Compare Ukrainian царина (caryna).

parole.significato: to take or find shelter, hide
parole.testo: Unknown. Often considered to derive from a hypothetical Vulgar Latin root *accubilare, but this does not work on a phonetic basis. Most likely derived from Latin cieō, ciere (“put in motion, act; summon, call”) or acciō, accīre (“summon, call for, fetch”), with a later change in conjugation. It was

Either from a Vulgar Latin root *adiliare, from Latin ilia or more likely from a Vulgar Latin root *adoliāre, from Latin adolēre (“burn; hence turn to vapor”), possibly through an early Romanian form *aduia. Another theory suggests a Latin root *aduliāre, from adulārī.

Either from Vulgar Latin *adiectāre, or *aiectāre, from Latin ēiectāre, all ultimately from iactus. Normally the i would shift to a j in Romanian, but it may have originally disappeared due to preceding the e, as in quiētus > (în)cet, and came back in speech over time due to a lack of consonants bet

From a Vulgar Latin root *aiūnāre, from adiūnāre, from Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare Aromanian agiun, agiunari, Spanish ayunar, French jeûner, also Italian digiunare. Cf. Albanian agjëroj, agjinoj. Alternatively borrowed from Gheg-Albanian agjinoj, a dialectical formation based on

Probably from Latin alica through a Vulgar Latin root *alaca (compare Spanish álaga), or alternatively from Hungarian alakor, but this itself has no other explanation than being derived from Romanian, unless, formally less likely, connected to the Hurro-Urartian family of Arabic خُلَّر (ḵullar). Either from alb + -eață or from a Vulgar Latin root *albitia, from albities, from Latin albus. Compare Aromanian algheatsã.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin alvea or albea, from Latin alveus (“channel or bed of a river”). Alternatively, formed as a new singular from the plural of an original Romanian masculine form *albiu. Compare Lombard albio, Venetan albio, albi, Tarantino albi, Piedmontese arbi, French auge.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *allentāre, from Latin lentus, or from *allenitāre, from lentis.

parole.significato: to make dizzy, flustered, intoxicated, stun
parole.testo: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *ammatīre, from Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), from Latin madidus or *maditus, from madere (“be wet”) (cf. Italian ammattire (“to go crazy, insane”), matto (“insane, mad, crazy”)). Alternatively, from a Vulgar Latin root *ammatteāre (with a later change of con

parole.significato: flint; piece of steel struck to produce sparks and light a fire
parole.testo: Either from Latin manuārius or manuāle or less likely a Vulgar Latin *ignārium, from ignis. Compare also mâner.

parole.significato: to become mute, lose the ability to speak
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *ammūtīre, itself either from Latin mūtus or from obmūtēscere; alternatively from the variant form, from *mutīre < mūtēscere, or simply derived from mut. Compare Aromanian amutsãscu, amutsãri, Italian ammutire.
Inherited from Latin illac ce, or alternatively Vulgar Latin *ad hocce, from ad + hoc.
Probably from arc + -ar or possibly from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, alteration of arcuārius (“maker of bows”), from Latin arcus.
Probably from arde + -ei. Other theories suggest deriving from the plural of an extinct diminutive word *ardel, or from a Vulgar Latin root *ardivus, ultimately from Latin ardeō.

Inherited from Latin ēricius, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”). The expected normal result would have been *ariț, and explanations for the current form include an intermediate Vulgar Latin *ērix, ēricis or alternatively *ēriciō, ēriciōnem, in which case it would be regressively derived

parole.significato: throw (to cause an object to move rapidly through the air), cast, hurl
parole.testo: Either from Latin ēruncāre or from a + Latin runcāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk-. Another theory proposes a Vulgar Latin *averruncāre (“to distance that which is bad”), which is less likely. Compare Aromanian aruc, arucari, Megleno-Romanian runc, Occitan arronçar, Spanish arrancar.
Either from the variant form răduce, from Latin redūcere, or from a Vulgar Latin root *arredūcere. Obsolete, used mostly before the 18th century. Compare the borrowed doublet reduce.

Several hypotheses exist; one most often proposed is Vulgar Latin *arrēctāre (whence also Portuguese arreitar and Neapolitan arrezzà/arrizzà), from Latin rēctus (“straight”), but the phonetic evolution would be irregular in this case; another possibility is Latin ratāre, as a frequentative of reor (

Possibly a substratum word or more likely from a Vulgar Latin root *arciārium or *arceārius, itself probably from Latin acer (“maple tree”), or alternatively derived from or influenced by arcus (“bows”), as many bows were made from this wood.

Unknown. Possibly from a change in conjugation from the form asmuța, from a Vulgar Latin root *exmucciāre (with variant form amuța from a *ammucciāre; cf. dialectal French amoisser); alternatively from a *assubmotiāre, or *ammotiāre, from Latin motus. Cf. also sumuța, which may be related.

From a Vulgar Latin root *assurdīre, itself either from Latin surdus or obsurdescere. Compare Aromanian asurdzãscu, asurdzãri, Italian assordire, French assourdir. Cf. also Portuguese ensurdecer, Spanish ensordecer.

parole.significato: to cover in a thin layer of gold
parole.testo: Either from aur or from a Vulgar Latin root *aurīre, from Latin aurēscere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assediāre, from Latin sedeō, or possibly from sedium. Compare Aromanian ashedz, ashidzari, French asseoir and Spanish asear.

Compare Aromanian bardzu (“white (of horses and mules)”): both it and the Romanian word may derive from Proto-Albanian *bardza (“white”), akin to Albanian bardhë (“white”). Another theory suggests that its origin is a Vulgar Latin root *gardea, from Latin ardea (compare Spanish garza (“heron”), Port

Either from berbec + -ar or from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vervēcārius, from Latin vervēx (Also attested as Medieval Latin birbicārius or berbicārius). Compare French berger, Sardinian berbecarju, berbecàlgiu, berbegarzu, Aromanian birbicar.
Either from beție + -iv or from an older bețiu, from Vulgar Latin root *bibitivus, from Latin bibitus, from bibō.

Either from the verb blestema or from a Vulgar Latin root *blastemium, from blasphemium, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin blasphemia. Compare Italian bestemmia, Old French blastenge, Old Occitan blastenh, Aromanian blãstem. Compare also blasfemie, a possible doublet.
From boci + -et, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *vōcitum, ultimately from Latin vōx. Compare Aromanian boatsit.

parole.significato: to bemoan, bewail, lament, mourn for
parole.testo: From boace or from a Vulgar Latin root *vōcīre, from alteration of *vōceāre, from Latin vōx, possibly influenced by vagīre. Compare Aromanian butsescu, butsiri; cf. also Italian bociare, Spanish vocear.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *abhorrīre, from Latin abhorrēre. A number of other inherited terms display dropping of the expected initial "a", e.g: animālia > ... > *anămaie > nămaie. Alternatively, but less likely, from Romani

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *botum, perhaps from Latin botulus or from a root *botium, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). Compare Italian bozza, French bosse. See also butuc
From boteza or from a Vulgar Latin *baptidiōnem, derived from Late Latin baptidiāre (“to baptize”), of Ancient Greek origin. Compare Aromanian pãtigiuni.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; alternatively
parole.testo: Compare Megleno-Romanian brǫndză and Aromanian brãndzã. Of uncertain origin: * Often considered to be a substrate word. * Other theories suggest, on the basis of what is used to make cheese, a derivation from Latin brandeum (originally meaning a linen covering, later a thin cloth for relic storage)

Unknown. Possibly a substrate word, perhaps from or related to Ruthenian or Ukrainian буба (buba, “swelling”) (cf. Bulgarian and Serbo-Croatian буба (buba, “insect pupa, bug, silkworm”), also Albanian bubë), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *buba from Late Latin būbō, būbōnēs, from Ancient Greek

parole.significato: to delight, to cheer, to indulge
parole.testo: * Possibly borrowed from Albanian bukur (“nice, beautiful”), but semantic difficulties exist. * Alternatively, a substrate Dacian or other Paleo-Balkanic word, akin to Albanian. * Another possible theory suggests a Vulgar Latin root *voculāre (“to call, yell”), from Latin vōcula, from vōx (“voice”),

parole.significato: ambling, or walking using both legs on one side at the same time
parole.testo: Uncertain; multiple theories exist. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *boiester, from Latin boia (“fetter”) (referring to the gait of the horse). Other proposed etymologies include Vulgar Latin *bovestris, a derivative of Latin bos, bovis; from Latin ambo extra; from a root *ambulester, from ambulō. Alte
Possibly from Vulgar Latin root *volvicāre, from Latin volvere, or from bulbuc.

Either from the above word or from a Vulgar Latin *avunus, ultimately from the same Proto-Indo-European root as avus. (Compare the diminutive avunculus, avonculus), probably influenced by or confused with bonus. Compare also Friulian von (“grandfather”), Calabrian and Piedmontese bona (“grandmother”

parole.significato: to insert, put in, put into
parole.testo: Either a substrate word or from a Vulgar Latin root *begāre, from Late Latin bīgāre, from Latin bīga (“chariot”), from bis iuga ("two yokes"). In this case, the original meaning may have been the now archaic one of "to yoke animals", later taking on broader or more abstract senses. The semantic deve
From a Vulgar Latin root *barbilia, from Latin barba, or alternatively from Romanian barbă + -ie. Compare Spanish barbijo and Italian barbiglio.

parole.significato: carpet beater (stick used to beat carpets and other things to clean off dust)
parole.testo: From bate + -tor, or from a Vulgar Latin root *batt(u)ātōrium, from Latin battuō.
From bate + -ătură, or from Vulgar Latin battetura, from Latin battuō. Compare Italian battitura.

From cel, itself an aphaeretic form of acel + alt, itself from Vulgar Latin *altru, a variant of alter, with an epenthetic -l- in all forms either for ease of pronunciation due to two adjacent vowels, cf. tale, mele, or due to the fact that it may descend from a Latin composition *eccum illum illum

parole.significato: a bucket in which milk curdles
parole.testo: From cheag + -ar, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *clagorium, ultimately from Latin coagulum, following metathesis, syncopation, and addition of a suffix. Compare Albanian kljuar.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *centipollium, from Latin centipellium, centipellio (“third stomach of a ruminant”) < centum + pellium, as bagpipes were made from animal stomachs. Compare also Italian centopelle (“tripe”). Alternatively from the variant form cimpoaie, perhaps from an earlier *șimp

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *cicculum, diminutive of Latin ciccum, or alternatively a derivative of Romanian ciuc, cognate to Albanian çukë, with South Slavic and Baltic cognates as well. See Proto-Slavic *čuka. The reconstructed root referred to sharp points.

parole.significato: sieve, sifter, strainer, screen, tammy, riddle
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cibrum, from Latin crībrum (through dissimilation). Compare Aromanian tsir; compare also the different dissimilation in French crible and Portuguese crivo. Alternatively from Latin cilibrum, an earlier or archaic form of cribrum (cf. Sardinian chilibru, chiliru), found i

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *cōnflexīre, from Latin flexus. Alternatively, an expressive formation from an earlier coflești < cofleșci, formed from fleșcăi with an expressive prefix co- (as in cocârja, copleși, cotropi, etc.) The least likely etymology proposed is a Vulgar Latin confr

Possibly inherited from Late Latin cattus (“cat”), having later been suffixed with -oi (or perhaps directly from a Vulgar Latin cattōneus), the original pronunciation thus being *cătoi. The change from ă to o is not uncommon, occuring in words such as; porumb < părumb and boteza < *băteza. See also
Unknown. Probably an expressive creation, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *contorpīre, from Latin contorpere, from torpere, or alternatively a Common Slavic *otrabiti (“to cut”).

Probably from Latin cerebrum, through a Vulgar Latin root *crebrum (which would have initially yielded *creur in Romanian before undergoing further changes; the -eie- may be due to a chip between two -r-'s, or unetymological; cf. also greier). Alternatively, possibly from the diminutive form cerebel

Uncertain. Probably a substratum word. Other theories include a Vulgar Latin root *curtiāre (“cut”), from Latin curtāre, or a *cruciāre (“cross”), from crux or a *curatiāre; alternatively, there may be a connection with Slavic *krotiti (compare ocroti). Compare also the likely related Albanian kurse
Probably an internal derivative of frânge with the prefix cu-, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *confrangere, from Latin confringere.

Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *cotītus (“sharpened”), from *cotīre (“sharpen”), from Latin cōs, cōtis (“whetstone”), or from *acutitus, from *acutīre, from acūtus (“sharp”). Compare Aromanian cutsut, cãtsut. Also, cf. ascuțit, cute.

parole.significato: plain (an expanse of land with relatively low relief)
parole.testo: Either from câmp (“field”) + -ie or from Vulgar Latin *campia, from Ancient Greek [Term?]. Compare Sicilian campia and Calabrian (?) campia; less likely from Latin campus + -inea.

parole.significato: young horse (up to three years old)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *caballānus, diminutive of Latin caballus, or from carnalis. Compare also Spanish carnero. Scriban (1939) proposes Transylvanian Saxon Jêrlänk, which is cognate to German Jährling and English yearling. Other theories include a Slavic *kъrdlanъ or a pre-Roma
From cădea + -ință, or possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin *cadentia, from Latin cadēns, present participle of cadō. If so, a doublet of cadență.

parole.significato: a ritual acrobatic dance performed by members of a Romanian secret fraternal society
parole.testo: Either from the above word or possibly from Vulgar Latin *collusium (“secret agreement, understanding”), from Latin collūsus < colludō.

parole.significato: hazel or medium/light brown (with a yellow or greenish tinge)
parole.testo: From capră (“goat”) + -ui, or possibly representing a Vulgar Latin *caprūneus, from caprūnus (cf. Occitan cabrun), ultimately from Latin capra.

From car + -uță or from Latin carruca, possibly from an original early Romanian result *cărucă and its plural *căruce (altered by influence from the diminutive suffix), or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin root *carrucia, *carrucea. Compare Aromanian cãrutsã. Cf. also Italian carrozza, Friulian c

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *cautelinus (with metathesis), from Latin cautēla, or alternatively from Latin continue or continuō (“continuously”), forms of continuus (compare similar phonetic change in către < contra); the normal result in Romanian would have been *cătinu, to which the suffix -

Inherited from Latin captō, captāre. Phonetically, it may have resulted from the merger of more than one Latin word originally; the variant form căta is likely derived from the Vulgar Latin form *cattāre (compare Spanish and Portuguese catar, Venetan catar), but various other etymologies have been p

Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *devocāre, from *devacuāre, from Latin vacuus, or from the form dezvoca, from a root *disvocāre. Compare Aromanian dizvoc, dizvucari, see also Romanian desfăca. Cf. Logudorese Sardinian bogare (“to take out, extract”), Campidanese debogada, Old French voiier (“t
From des- + jug or from a Vulgar Latin root *disiugāre, from Latin dis- + iugāre. Compare deiugāre. Cf. also Aromanian dizgiug, dizgiugari and Italian disgiogare.

parole.significato: to remove, move away, move to a distance
parole.testo: From departe. Alternatively and less likely, from a Vulgar Latin root *dequartāre, from Latin quartus, as with French écarter from *exquartāre or from departior.

From a Vulgar Latin root *disculceus, itself either from a shortening of Late Latin disculceātus, disculciātus, or from *discalceus (from Latin dis- + calceus), and influenced by the -u- in disculciō; alternatively from a variant of Romanian descălța. Compare Aromanian discultsu, Friulian discolç, V
From des- + înfășa or possibly a Vulgar Latin *disfasciāre, from Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia (“band, strip”). Compare Aromanian disfash, disfãshari.

parole.significato: to unfold, unfurl, unwrap, open up
parole.testo: From des- + înfășura, or possibly a Vulgar Latin root *disfasciolāre, from Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia (“band, strip”).

Either from a Vulgar Latin root *distramāre, from Latin trama or from des- + *tramă, which likely once existed as an inherited term in old/early Romanian (and also survived in Aromanian tramã) but now exists only as a neologism borrowed from French (cf. tramă). See also stramă. Compare Aromanian dis

parole.significato: to uncork, clear, open, clear obstructions from
parole.testo: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *distuppāre, from Latin stuppa, or from the prefix des- + [a]stupa. Compare Aromanian distup, distupari, French détouper.

parole.significato: to part, sever, divide, disjoin, disunite
parole.testo: Unknown. One proposed etymology starts with the variant (now mostly regional or archaic) form, desghina, and has it modified and crossed with îmbina through analogy in relatively modern times. The word desghina, which has an Aromanian cognate, dizgjlin, dizgljinari (“to cut branches”), has been trac
From dez- + (îm)brăca, or from Vulgar Latin *disbracāre, from Latin brāca.

parole.significato: to give up, stop or break off (a bad habit)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a hypothetical *dezbăiera, from baieră, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *disvēlāre, from Latin vēlum.

parole.significato: to untie, unbind, loose, unloosen, unfasten
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin disligāre, from Latin dis- + ligō (“tie, bind”). Alternatively, an internal formation from dez- + lega. Compare Aromanian dizleg, dizligari, Friulian disleâ, Venetan desligar, Italian slegare, French délier, Catalan deslligar, Spanish and Portuguese desligar

parole.significato: to cause to change one's mind
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *dismantāre, from mantāre, intensive of Latin maneō, or from *dismentāre, from mens, mentis.

From a Vulgar Latin root *disvolvere, from Latin dis- + volvere, or alternatively from Romanian des- + (în)voalbe (on the basis of deschide-închide, descărca-încărca, desfunda-înfunda, etc.). Compare Spanish desenvolver, also Italian svolgere.

parole.significato: to remove all the contents of something, clear, drive out, evacuate (a place)
parole.testo: From deșert, or possibly from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin root *dēsertāre, from Latin dēsertus. Compare Italian disertare. Doublet of dezerta, which was borrowed.
From de *mâneață, from Vulgar Latin *mānitia, or from Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”) + the Romanian suffix -eață. Compare Aromanian dimineatsã.

Borrowed from Greek ντουζίνα (ntouzína), from Neapolitan duzzina (“dozen”), either from Occitan dotzena or French douzaine (or the corresponding ancestor languages), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *dōdeci and Latin duodecim.

Unknown. Possibly from Vulgar Latin root *derapināre / *deripināre, or from Latin deruncināre, the present active infinitive of deruncinō (“to plane off, level, shave”), probably via an intermediate form *deru(n)quināre, as qu → p is a common sound shift.
From ferice, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *fēlīcāre, from Latin fēlīx.
From fiert + -tură, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *fertura, contraction of *fervitura, derived from *fervitus, as a variant past participle of Latin ferveō. Compare Aromanian hirturã.

A back-formation from înfiora, itself either from a Vulgar Latin *infebrizō or later Balkan Romance equivalent, derived from Latin febris. Cognate to Aromanian hior, also compare heavrã the Aromanian term directly inherited from febris.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *flacula, from Latin facula (“little torch”), from fax (“torch”), or possibly influenced by Latin flamma. Probably a doublet of fachie. Compare Italian fiaccola. Compare also Albanian flakë, Gallo-Italic of Sicily ciàccara (“torch”)

Fuller form in dialectal fluieră, of uncertain or disputed origin; possibly from Latin flātūrālis (adj.) ‘blowing’, from flātūra ‘act of blowing’. Other theories suggest a Vulgar Latin root *flibula, from fibula (compare sense of flute in Latin tibia), or a derivative of the related verb fluiera, or

Related to fluier; it is disputed whether the noun was derived from the verb or vice-versa. Some other proposed theories include a Vulgar Latin root *flaulāre, or a derivative of Latin flāre, or alternatively of ultimately imitative origin.

Probably ultimately from Latin famelicus, through a Vulgar Latin root *flamenicus, or alternatively from a root *famulentus, from famēs (compare Portuguese famulento), through an intermediate form *flamuentus. A less likely origin is flammabundus. Compare Megleno-Romanian flămund.
From foc + -ar or possibly Vulgar Latin *focārium, nominalization of the Late Latin adjective focārius, from Latin focus. Compare French foyer, from which the modern senses of the word were derived.
Either from foaie + -i or from a Vulgar Latin root *follīre, from Late Latin follēre, from Latin follis.

parole.significato: a small bellows or a small sack made from an animal stomach
parole.testo: From foale or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *follicellus from Latin folliculus, diminutive of follis.
Either from Vulgar Latin root *fragidus, from Latin fragilis or more likely from fracidus (presumably altered from an earlier form *fraced).

parole.significato: a metal or wooden rod on which meat is stuck when roasted; skewer, spit
parole.testo: Either from frige or from a Vulgar Latin root *frigālis or *frigāria, from Latin frigō.

parole.significato: roast (a cut of meat suited to roasting)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus, or from fript, past participle of frige. Compare Aromanian fripturã, Italian frittura, French friture.

Probably from the variant fuioară, from Vulgar Latin root *foliola, from Latin folium, or alternatively from *folliōlus, from follis, or *funiolus, from funiculus. Compare Aromanian fuljor, compare also Albanian fjollë.

parole.significato: a bifurcation, branching, split, division (especially of a mountain chain)
parole.testo: From furcă + -tură, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *furcatūra, from Latin furca.

parole.significato: person who makes or sells spindles
parole.testo: From fus + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *fusārius, from Latin fūsus.
From fân + -eață, or from a Vulgar Latin root *fenicia, from Latin fenum.
From fag + -et, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *fagetum, from Latin fagus. Compare Aromanian fãdzet, Italian faggeto, Asturian fayéu.

From *glara, possibly from German Kralle, following metathesis, or alternatively possibly a substratum word; another theory is that it perhaps derives from a hypothetical intermediate *înghiare, from a Vulgar Latin root *unglaris < *ungularis, from Latin ungula.

parole.significato: to shell, pod; to remove grains from corn/maize, to shuck
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Latin glabrāre, from glaber (“smooth”). Related to dezgheura / dejgheura, itself sometimes considered to derive from a Vulgar Latin root *disglabrāre, or from *disgluberāre, from glubō. Alternatively, related to gheară.

Possibly a substratum word, akin to or derived from Albanian gjemb, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *pungulus, from Latin pungō (compare Italian pungolo) through intermediate roots *punglu > *glumpu through metathesis > *ghiumpu > ghimp(u).

Probably from the feminine variant form ghioacă, from Vulgar Latin root *cloca, following metathesis and syncopation of Latin cochlea, or possibly related to găoace (“snail, egg, or nut shell”), from *gău (from Latin cavum) + suffix -oc.
Related to or derived from ghioc, or alternatively perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *glaucellus, a derivative of Latin glaucus (“bright, sparkling, gleaming”).

Possibly a substrate word, akin to Albanian gurmaz, or derived from the Albanian or from Vulgar Latin gruma (a variant of Latin grumus attested as meaning a nipple or teat but possibly also a small hill) + the Romanian suffix -ză. Compare also Italian gruma and Aromanian gurmadz.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gratārium, from *gratis, itself a variant of Latin crātis or alternatively from *gratālis, derived from the same root.

parole.significato: a disease of the liver affecting sheep (ovines) and bovines
parole.testo: Unknown. Often considered either a substratum term or derived from Albanian këlbazë, gëlbazë. Another theory suggests the Albanian may instead be a borrowing from a local Romanian or Eastern Romance language (compare Aromanian gãlbadzã), and that the word derives ultimately from a Vulgar Latin clave
Either from a hypothetical root *gău, from Latin cavum, or from a Vulgar Latin root *cavō, cavōnem, from cavum. See also gaură, găvan, văgăună.
From inel + -ar or from Vulgar Latin *anellārius, from Latin anellus.

Probably from Late Latin medietās, medietātem (from Latin medius), through an intermediate Vulgar Latin root *diemitātem or *diumitātem through metathesis or from dimidietās, dimidietātem (compare Portuguese metade, French moitié). The first element of the word may be linked to or influenced by an A

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *juglāre, syncopated form of Latin jugulāre, iugulāre (“to slay, to slit (someone’s) throat”), with a nasal infix added later, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin intermediate root *junglāre < *jungulāre. Compare Aromanian giunglju, giungljari.
Either made as a singular from laturi, plural of lat, or from Latin latera, plural of latus (“side, flank”) (through a Vulgar Latin root; compare Old Italian latora). Less likely from Latin lateris.
Unknown. Usually thought to be a back formation of legăna, or from Vulgar Latin root *lecanis, from Ancient Greek λεκάνη (lekánē). Per Paliga, a substrate word. Compare Aromanian leagãn.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *ligināre, from Latin ligāre (“tie”) or from leagăn.

parole.significato: a multitude of wood or timber
parole.testo: From lemn or from a Vulgar Latin or Early Medieval Latin lignāmen, from Latin lignum. Compare Italian legname, Spanish leñame.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lispida, from Ancient Greek λίσπος (líspos, “smooth, polished”). Or alternatively, possibly from Latin lapidem (“stone, tombstone”).
From lumina + -ciune or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *lūminātiō, *lūminātiōnem, from Latin lūminō, lūmina.
From larg or from Vulgar Latin *largīre, from Latin largīrī.
Probably from an earlier form *mirune, from a Vulgar Latin *miriō, *miriōnem, from Latin mīror; alternatively derived from Romanian mira, perhaps through a verb *miruna.
Either from minți + -tor or from Vulgar Latin *mentitor, from Latin mentior. Compare Italian mentitore, French menteur.
Feminine form of mior, itself probably from miel + the diminutive -or, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *agnelliōlus (feminine *agnelliōla), from Latin agnellus, agnella.
Either from a diminutive of miel, derived as a masculine form from mioară, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *agnelliōlus, from Latin agnellus. Compare Aromanian njior.

parole.significato: to move (a body part, an object)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from the Vulgar Latin root *miscicāre, *mixticāre, from Latin miscīre ("to agitate, mix") or from a derivative of miscēre.

parole.significato: a moo (sound made by a cow)
parole.testo: Either from the verb mugi + -et or from Latin mūgītus (through a Vulgar Latin *mūgĭtus).

Unknown. Starting from the dialectal variant form mucica, possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *muticāre, from Latin mutīre, a parallel formation of mussāre "to murmur" (compare Spanish amusgar, from *mussicāre). It may have referred to the growl of an animal before biting. Another etymology may be *mu

Unknown. Cognate to Aromanian mãtsucã. Often considered to be from the Vulgar Latin root *matteūca, itself from *mattea or Latin mateola + a suffix *-ūca, of possibly Gallic origin (compare French massue, Occitan maçuga, Portuguese maça, machuca, Old Galician-Portuguese massuca, Italian mazza, mazzo

Probably ultimately from Ancient Greek μανδραγόρας (mandragóras). Compare the Albanian cognate matërgonë and Hungarian nadragulya. It may have arrived via a Vulgar Latin intermediate root *mandragona. Compare Spanish martagón. Alternatively, and less likely, from a substratum or Dacian source.

Unknown. Compare Italian nastro. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *nastula, from Proto-West Germanic *nastilu, or alternatively borrowed from the Italian word several centuries ago in the early modern era, originally in a form *nastru, with a plural *nastruri, with the loss of the first -r- and mad

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *niglīna < *nigellīna (compare Megleno-Romanian migľină), from Late Latin nigella, from Latin nigellus (compare French nielle), or from a root *nigrīna, ultimately from niger. Alternatively, possibly related to năgară and neg.

parole.significato: to engage in trade, buy and sell
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *negōtiāre, from Latin negōtiārī, or alternatively derived from the noun negoț. Doublet of negocia.

Several theories exist: from a Vulgar Latin root *nōda, resulting either from Latin nōdus crossed with or influenced by coadă in Romanian, or from Latin nates crossed with coda. Compare Aromanian noadã (“member, penis”).

Likely formed analogically with a feminine suffix from the older form nor, from Vulgar Latin *nŏrus, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós. Compare Aromanian norã. Alternatively, like most of the other Romance cognates, derived from a Vulgar Latin form *nŏra, althou
Either from oaie + -ar or from a Vulgar Latin *oviārius, from Latin ovis. Compare Aromanian uiar.

parole.significato: to grope/poke/fumble about, feel one's way about
parole.testo: From an earlier orbeca, from orb or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *orbicāre, from Latin orbus.
From ou + -a or from a Vulgar Latin *ōvāre, from Latin ōvum. Compare Aromanian oauã, Friulian ovâ, Portuguese and Spanish ovar.

Unknown. Possibly linked to Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion) (cf. Latin pittacium (“label; patch”)), or from a Vulgar Latin root *piticus. Compare Aromanian peaticã (“rag, scrap, patch”), peatic/peaticu, Calabrian pettica ("leather band, strip"); cf. also Spanish pedazo (“piece”). See also pitac.

parole.significato: the skin of an animal, especially a young lamb
parole.testo: From piele + -cea or from Vulgar Latin root *pellicella, a diminutive of Latin pellis.
Unknown. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *pillum (compare piuă, from *pilla), or from Latin pīlum (“spear”).

Cf. Bulgarian похлупка (pohlupka). Alternatively derived from the earlier forms pleopă and plopă (now regional variants), from a Vulgar Latin *pluppa, metathesis of *pupla, from a contraction of Latin pūpula (“pupil”). Compare the transition from Latin populus to Romanian plop (which also has a vari
Diminutive of plămân (“lung”) or plămânare, another name for the herb. This may be derived from Vulgar Latin *pulmōnāris for Latin pulmōnārius, or from pulmōnāria, all ultimately from pulmō (“lung”).

From popor + -an, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin populānus, from Latin populus (compare Italian popolano). Alternatively, an early borrowing from the Italian. However, it has been attested since the early 17th century and may be a popular or hereditary term.

parole.significato: to invite; to welcome, treat hospitably
parole.testo: From ospăta, perhaps influenced by proaspăt (compare prospătură (“fresh food”)) or preceded by the suffix pre, or alternatively possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *perhospitāre < Late Latin hospitō < Latin hospes.

Either from feminine of pucios, from puți or from a Vulgar Latin root *puteōsa, from Latin puteō. Compare Italian puzzoso. Cf. also the name of the Italian city Pozzuoli, from the Latin name Puteoli, referring to the sulfuric smell in the area.

parole.significato: stinking, smelly, having a foul odor or smell, especially of sulfur
parole.testo: From puți + -os or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *puteōsus, from Latin puteō. Compare Italian puzzoso.

Inherited from Latin pullus, probably through a Vulgar Latin root *pulleus, or alternatively formed from the plural of an original Romanian form *pul. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”). Compare Spanish pollo and Italian pollo.

From a Vulgar Latin root *pūrōnium, from Latin pūs, pūris, from Proto-Italic *pūs, from Proto-Indo-European *púH-os ~ *púH-es-os, from *puH-. Compare Aromanian pronjiu. Alternatively from a root *pur, derived from this Latin root, and with the suffix -oi added within proto-Romanian.
Probably from Vulgar Latin root *putina, from Ancient Greek πυτίνη (putínē, “flask”), or from a Vulgar Latin *buttina, from Latin buttis (cf. Germanic butinna, borrowed from Latin, German Büttner).

Various theories exist. Either diminutive of pulă (“dick”), or from Vulgar Latin root *pūtium (compare prepuț), from Old Latin pūtos (“penis”), or from root *pubucea, from Latin pubes, or from Vulgar Latin putta, feminine of puttus, superlative of putus. See Spanish and Portuguese puta. Cognate with
Probably from a Vulgar Latin root *pandea, from a crossing of Latin pannus and brandeum, or from a *pannea, from pannus, or alternatively related to pandō.

parole.significato: hawthorn (especially Crataegus monogyna or Crataegus oxyacantha)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *peducellus, itself either from peduculus (“louse”), diminutive of Latin pēdis, or a variant of pedicellus (“small louse”) through analogy with or influence from peduculus. Compare Italian pedicello.

parole.significato: to delouse, get rid of lice (from the hair, body, etc.)
parole.testo: From păduche or possibly from Vulgar Latin *peduclāre < pēduculāre, from Latin pediculāre.
Either from păduche + -os, or from Vulgar Latin peduclōsus, from Latin peduculōsus, variant of pēdīculōsus analogous to peduculus. Compare Aromanian piducljos.
From pădure + -os or from Latin palūdōsus (through a metathesized Vulgar Latin form *padūlōsus). Compare paludos, a borrowed doublet. Compare Aromanian pãduros.

parole.significato: a thin veil or shroud; a fine weaving of flax, silk, or cotton
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *palliōla, from Latin pallia < pallium, or from the plural of palliōlum.

parole.significato: an old unit of measurement for cereals
parole.testo: From pătrar, from patru. Alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *quartāria, from Latin quartārius.

parole.significato: to chop off, cut off, hew off, lop off, sever, dock, cut
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from Common Slavic *rězati (“shorten”), but this presents phonetic difficulties. Another possibility may be a Vulgar Latin root *retizāre (“cut branches hanging above water”) < Latin retae, or *retundiāre (compare French rogner), or from Ancient Greek αἱρετίζω (hairetízō) ("to choos

Uncertain. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *rhizomāre, from Ancient Greek ῥίζα (rhíza, “root, base, foundation”)—compare Greek ρίζωμα (rízōma, “rhizome”). Alternatively through metathesis, from a Vulgar Latin root *remediāre, from Latin remedium. Compare Aromanian aradzim, arãdzimari.
From rugi + -et or from Latin rūgītus (through a Vulgar Latin *rugĭtus).

Probably from Vulgar Latin *aerūgina, from Latin aerūgō, aerūginem (“copper rust”), with a later stress shift to the penultimate syllable in Romanian, which may have occurred due to the influence of derivatives such as rugini, ruginos, etc. Compare Italian ruggine, Friulian ruzin; cf. also Asturian

Probably from rece + -oare. Compare Aromanian arcoari. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *recor or from Latin rigor, rigorem, which had an attested use of "cold" (compare Sardinian arragore (“frost”)).

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *rasclāre, from *resticulāre, from Latin resticula. Alternatively, from Bulgarian расшивам (rasšivam). The result may be due to dissimilation from a form *răsșia, as with rășchira.

Either from Serbo-Croatian čkȃlj / чка̑љ (thistle) (although difficult on phonetic grounds) or more likely from a Vulgar Latin *squaleus (later reduced to *scalius), from Latin squaleo. Cf. Spanish escajo, Portuguese escalheiro. Less likely from Greek σκαλίας (skalías).
From s- + cufunda (“to sink”), or from Vulgar Latin *excōnfundāre, from Latin cōnfundō (“found”), from fundus (“bottom”). Compare Sicilian scuffundare.

parole.significato: to get up, stand up, rise
parole.testo: Unknown. Generally considered to be from a Vulgar Latin *excubulāre (a term used in hunting, meaning to remove from an animal's den or nest), but this is a difficult link to make semantically and phonetically. Another possibility is a link to a Latin root *collāre, from Ancient Greek (compare Italia

parole.significato: nappy, diaper (an absorbent garment worn by a baby, or by someone who is incontinent.)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Slavic *skutъ, or from Vulgar Latin *scuticum, from Latin scutica (“a leather lash, whip”) (itself borrowed from Ancient Greek σκύτος (skútos)), and probably confused with derivatives of cutis (“leather”) (compare cutica). Therefore, the meaning could have changed from a leath
From scânteie, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *scantiliāre or *scintiliāre, from Latin scintillō, scintillāre. Compare Aromanian scãntiljedz, scãntiljari.

parole.significato: to strike (a light), make sparks, scintillate
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *excapulāre (compare Italian scapolare, Spanish escabullir) or from Latin ex + caperāre. Compare Aromanian ascapir, ascãpirari.

parole.significato: to decline, go down, go under, set, be on the wane
parole.testo: Possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin excapitāre (which meant "decapitate" in its attested form, but the Romance descendants may derive from an unattested sense of "to conclude, finish, reach the end of" which developed later, or possibly "to decrease, diminish"), ultimately from Latin
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *exfracticāre, from Latin fractus or alternatively from Romanian sfert.
Unknown. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *expavīmen, from Latin expavere, from pavor (“fear”). Or possibly has a connection to spasma, spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”).

From a Vulgar Latin root *supercenna, from *supergenna, formed from a confusion of Latin supercilia and gena (whence came Romanian geană), or from supercilia with influence from geană in early Romanian or Proto-Romanian, analogous to the original Latin deriving from super (“above”) + cilia (“eyelash

parole.significato: with white spots on the head
parole.testo: Probably from stea or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *stēlleius or *stēlleus, ultimately from Latin stēlla.

From Byzantine Greek στέριφος (stériphos), borrowed from Vulgar Latin *exstirpus. Alternatively, directly from Vulgar Latin, from Latin exstirpo (“to root out”). Compare Aromanian sterpu, Albanian shterp, Sicilian strippa, Venetan sterpo, Friulian sterpe.

Probably a literary verbal derivation from stingheri. Less likely theories include Latin singularis contaminated with Romanian stingher, or from a Vulgar Latin *extraiugularium, from extra and iugum, iugulum, with the idea that this referred to solitary ox not part of a pair.

Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *styphus, from Late Latin stypa + typhe, from Ancient Greek τύφη (túphē), or possibly related to tufă and contaminated with stypa. It may also simply be from tufă with an initial expressive -s-. Not related to Hebrew סוּף (súf).

parole.significato: to roll up, tuck up, turn up
parole.testo: Unknown. Often considered to be from a Vulgar Latin root *subfollicāre, from Latin follis (“bellows”), but there are semantic and phonetic difficulties here; compare înfuleca. Alternatively, and perhaps more likely, from supplicāre, which fits the meaning more closely if one were to take the literal

From sughița, or possibly from Vulgar Latin suggluttium (attested in some glosses), ultimately from Latin singultus, and influenced by gluttiō. Compare Aromanian sugljits, Portuguese soluço, Spanish sollozo, Calabrian sogliuttu, suggiuttu, Sicilian sugghiuzzu. Compare also Italian singhiozzo, from *
Probably from sub + grumaz (compare sugușa), or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *suggrumāre, from Latin grumus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *submotiare, from Latin submōtus, from submoveō. Alternatively related to asmuți, cf. the variant amuța.

parole.significato: to defeat, vanquish, subdue, dominate, overwhelm
parole.testo: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *subvolvere, from Latin volvere (it is uncertain if the root is the same as the attested Latin verb subvolvere, present infinitive of subvolvō (“roll up, along, or uphill”), given the difference in meanings, or if it was simply a later construction); alternatively,

parole.significato: to shade, make or keep in the shade

From a Vulgar Latin root *anglariu, from contraction of Latin angulārius, from angulus (“angle, corner”), or from angulāris.

From zgăuri, plural of zgău, or from a Vulgar Latin root *excavulāre, from *cavula, from Latin cavus. Compare gaură.

parole.testo: From pană, or from a Vulgar Latin root *impinnare, from Latin pinna (“feather”).

parole.significato: to sew or spin with yarn or thread
parole.testo: From în- + fir or possibly from Vulgar Latin *infīlāre, from Latin fīlum. Compare Aromanian nhir, nhirari.
From a Vulgar Latin root *infolliāre, from Latin follis, or from foi, plural of foaie. Compare Aromanian nfoljiu, nfuljari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *infrontāre, from Latin frōns, or alternatively derived from frunte. Compare Aromanian nfruntu, nfruntari.

parole.significato: to leaf, produce leaves, cover with leaves or foliage
parole.testo: Either from în + frunză or from a Vulgar Latin root *infrondīre, from Latin frondēscere, from frons.
From a Vulgar Latin root *infollicāre, from Late Latin follicāre, from Latin follis, or alternatively from fullicāre, from fullo (“fuller”).

parole.significato: to clog, obstruct, stuff, stop up
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *infundāre, from Latin fundus or from în + fund.
